line: Misaeng: not yet alive. A group on a go board that is neither alive nor dead.
It started with a toy: his uncle's set of stones. The small boy couldn't leave them alone.
Go on, then. Where would you play?
beats.speaker: un

line: He said the word right, the first time. His uncle took him to the baduk class in the neighbourhood, and his mother was happy to pay.
He learned fast. Soon he held his own in his uncle's and his father's betting games, and won their money back from the man at the corner shop.
On the class director's advice he moved to an amateur six-dan's academy. Nobody could stop a nine-year-old who laid out book problems alone at dawn.
Genius. To his parents the word was a sweet hypnosis. They sent him to a professional's dojang, and they burned for it all the hotter because his father's company had just gone under.
At eleven he entered the Korea Baduk Association as a trainee. Around then his parents began clipping Lee Chang-ho's and Lee Sedol's rankings and prize money out of the newspapers.
Only now does he see his father's wrinkles, and how dull his mother's eyes have gone.

The world sheds its skin. He hasn't changed, he tells himself: tomorrow he'd still be here, losing to younger kids with higher rankings. Only the world in his eyes has changed. Blue and green have gone grey.

It wasn't talent. It wasn't bad luck, or losing by half a point again and again. It wasn't playing between part-time jobs, or parents who couldn't give him pocket money. It wasn't his father dying and his mother taking to her bed.
Those would hurt too much. So: it's not that I didn't try. But I'll say it's because I didn't try hard enough.
He walks away dropping stones from his pocket, a few at a time.
Kang Ho-ryong and Ahn Sang-gi turned pro last year. They were his friends in the trainee room.
You're really quitting? After everything you've put in?
beats.speaker: hy

line: He says nothing. They were friends. He's going because there's nothing else he can do.
He ties up his game records in bundles, and puts them out with the board.
They moved to the edge of the city on what was left of the deposit. The tripe restaurant failed; the shutters said for rent.

His mother worked on building sites until her body gave out. He studied for the high-school equivalency exam between part-time jobs. In winter she signed up for public-works jobs at the ward office. In the bathroom, he washed her back.

After the exam, at his sponsor's suggestion, he worked at the sponsor's company. At first his colleagues were curious. Baduk? What dan? Can you play blindfold? Then: why did you quit? Then: no flexibility. Look at this copy.
Failed trainees work at the association, or teach, or join an online baduk company, or report on games, or go to university. Only me.
Go and thank him. The president who gave you that job. You owe him that.
beats.speaker: mo

line: You took your time. ...I'm sorry about last time. At my place. That was uncomfortable for you.
beats.speaker: sp

line: I've talked to a friend. He runs a trading company. Only he knows about the baduk, and he'll keep it to himself. They've been told the ordinary things. It'll be a simple interview.
beats.speaker: sp

line: But your papers are thin for a regular hire. You'll come in with nothing on you. Some will call you a parachute.
beats.speaker: sp

line: The city has put its make-up on. Office workers fill the street: toasting, flattering, complaining, going home.
On the platform, and from the night bus along the expressway: start from the bottom, the way everyone else did. I won't fail again, the way I failed at baduk.
If there's a light I must keep burning, I'll answer for it. If there's a light allowed me. Is there one, for me?
One by one the lights gather, and light the night.
The first morning. The alarm. The alarm again.
He takes the alley stairs three at a time in his new suit. A struggling group from the very first move.
The department head's message: don't come to the office. Go straight to a café in Jongno. There's a buyer, and nobody else to meet him.
Oh Sang-sik, section head, Sales Team 3. Red eyes. Stubble. Three sons climbing on him on the sofa, and food pushed into his mouth at the table.
You only find out how heavy your body is, how heavy your life is, when you're thrown into it.
At night he sleeps on the floor under his wife and three boys, and apologises to someone in his sleep.
Last year he begged his department head for more people. Last month, buried in paper cups, he was promised them soon. Then the golf bag went out of the door.
Yesterday the boys woke him, and he took them hiking on a weekday. He managed to forget the Wednesday eleven o'clock meeting with an overseas buyer. On the summit, his phone rings.
Where are you? The buyer's waiting. If he walks, we both die.
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: Anyone can go, sir. The director. The executives. The president himself.
beats.speaker: oh

line: I've hired someone. A new man. He goes in your team first. When can you get there?
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: He runs down the mountain. Five hundred metres in thirty minutes on the road in.
There was a paper at the workshop. Fear is mostly irrational...
beats.speaker: oh

line: Shall I tell you about dismissal-notice pay?
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: Mangwon-dong crossroads. Twelve kilometres an hour. Eight to go. Thirty minutes late. Fear is rational.
beats.speaker: oh

line: I'm sending today's new hire straight to the meeting.
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: A rookie? On his first day? Sent down from upstairs?
beats.speaker: oh

line: Okada at the Japan branch says even a cat's paw would help. Are we in a position to be picky?
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: A café in Jongno. A buyer from overseas, and his Korean manager, Kang. Nobody from One International has come but a new hire with no papers.
He can't talk trade. He can talk one thing. He draws a problem on a sheet and slides it across the table.
A puzzle? All right. Black to play?
beats.speaker: by

line: Play inside. Let them take it. Take back more.
Oh Sang-sik bursts in, thirty minutes late, red-eyed, in hiking clothes under his jacket. He stops dead.
Your young man kept us busy. The quiz was fun.
beats.speaker: ks

line: No. I found it on the internet.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Oh's car. A battered laptop, an old phone, paper cups. Red eyes on the road.
Tissue. ...Kim. The Malaysian claim. The contract was FOB, the damage is in the wooden packing, that's the carrier. Push back. We're not suckers.
beats.speaker: oh

line: FOB. Claim. Certificate of origin. Jang understands none of it. But he knows how to read a man from his things.
He once lost a game to a trainee just like this: sloppy, red-eyed, bored-looking, glasses. He'd read him as careless. He was wrong.
Obsessive. Responsible. A man who carries everything.
A month on a desert island. That's all I want. ...You speak English? No? Sign up at a language school.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Oh nods at the wheel, and washes down a handful of vitamins.
The first day was a test. He passed it. Baduk helped, though he hid it.
In the lobby Oh shakes a managing director's hand, greets a deputy general manager, and needles the head of a rival team, and explains them all to Jang on the way to the lift.
Jang Geu-rae is an intern, attached to Sales Team 3. In two months there's a PT test.
beats.speaker: hr

line: One International: the trading arm of a group. He doesn't yet know what a trading company does.
I'm your mentor. Kim Dong-sik is your buddy.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Assistant manager Kim. Ask me anything. First: this requisition, to General Affairs. Supplies.
beats.speaker: kd

line: And greet people louder. Pitch it up. Sol!
beats.speaker: kd

line: A grey memory: an executive telling him he's a special case. No university, no specialty, picked by the owner's eye, an experiment. Build a specialty before the PT.
I came in from a provincial college on clubs and contest prizes. Nobody here cares where you're from. Once you're in, though, you're up against people with credentials.
beats.speaker: kd

line: General Affairs hands over a box of supplies: pens, sticky notes, a glue stick.
Sort these files into my folders. Check the numbers. Retype the reports.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Indonesian IT export proposals, folder after folder. He draws a mind map, designs a better tree, and makes new folders. It takes an afternoon.
Interns' study tonight. PT topics, rehearsals. And we find out who the dud is.
beats.speaker: gl

line: Where are my folders? Who do you think you are?
beats.speaker: kd

line: That structure is the company's. Everybody uses it. If you don't understand it, ask. This isn't work you do alone. It's work you do together.
beats.speaker: kd

line: When he was fifteen he filed his game records by tournament, by player, by opening. A system only he ever had to read.
Come on. It's how you learn the tricks of the job.
beats.speaker: gl

line: A bar full of interns. Topics are pitched and torn apart: numbers people against feelings people. The only woman is introduced. Ahn Young-yi.
Are we going to talk about the actual work?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: That's bar talk. This is PT prep. There's no trick to the work but time. You've got that much filing due tomorrow, and you're sitting here? Secure your own stones, then attack.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: He runs back to the office saying it over and over. He lived by that proverb his whole life, and he had to hear it from someone else.
His teacher at the board: however good the point, what use is it if your own stones die?
He really does have filing due. Come on. You're going to apologise.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Jang is at his desk, with the folders spread around him.
Sorry. I didn't know you had urgent work. Do it Kim's way. Familiar is efficient.
beats.speaker: gl

line: Ahn reads Jang's folder scheme over his shoulder.
It's rational. Anyone could use it, if they knew the categories. But only the staff share the old order. Change it when you're in charge.
beats.speaker: ms_ahn

line: You're doing fine. Don't worry so much.
beats.speaker: oh

line: The file's a settlement summary for a few executives, so date order is enough. But his cross-index has something. You keep a private re-sort anyway, don't you? Use it from the planning stage and related work across departments could line up. For a company this size, we're inefficient.
beats.speaker: ms_ahn

line: She kept herself alive, and him too. Both live.
That night, as after every game, he replays the day. He dreams of a board: rows of white stones, and one black. Baduk. It drives me mad.
He woke before the alarm. Yesterday's filing isn't done. The crush on the train.
Am I the only one still dreaming? The world is faster than me.
The trading teams work to their partners' clocks. The Americas team head is yelling at a junior: an offer sheet, a ten-day claim window, missed.
Ten days! Ten! ...I'm going to the sauna.
beats.speaker: am

line: On the frame strip, Black approaches and touches White. The hard fight in the office begins.
He catches himself making useless high-quality work, and makes it plain and safe instead.
Kim's B/L call to the forwarder. The copies. The floor. All at once.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Asleep? Set your priorities. The PT dates are fixed: first week of next month, at the training centre, a whole week. Individual tasks and a team task. Think about partners.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Who'd want a dud for a partner? ...We might work well together, you and I.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Choose carefully. You have everything the other interns want. No confidence, no grasp of the work, no skills.
beats.speaker: kd

line: With a dream team everybody scores. But if you're paired with a sure dud, you shine. A sacrificial lamb.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Be careful of whoever comes to you first.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Copies. Trays of snacks pushed at him: eat while you work. Bread alone at his desk. A senior takes him aside: bring it to me first, Oh hates obvious mistakes. A kindness that only makes more work.
Not going home? Got a partner?
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Whoever it is, trust them. The moment you see your partner as a rival, your own scheming shows. The one inside the board doesn't see it. Everyone watching does.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: A trainee at a board, ringed by onlookers. Everyone outside already knows.
If I trust my partner to the end, the judges outside will see me. It's not about choosing. Do your part, and trust the rest.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: A different view from Kim's, and a good one. But she's being judged too.
Put it in the cabinet. Who reads settlement files anyway? Next: re-sort this by quantity and check it against the purchase orders.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Han Seok-yul. They had me at the Ulsan plant; I came straight back when I heard about the PT.
beats.speaker: han

line: Taking sente: leading the game. Until now he has always handed it over. This time he leads.
Bad air up here. But a roof clears your head. I love factories. Ports. Airports.
beats.speaker: han

line: I joined half a month before you. Mechanical engineering. Contest prizes. I don't like tinkering, I like understanding a machine and getting it across. That's sales. That's trade. They sent me to Ulsan because I'm as good as hired. Plant tours, interviews, foreign buyers. I've even had a meal with the president!
beats.speaker: han

line: Stone after stone, slammed down in handfuls. Chase his moves and you end up a struggling group.
Team up with me. Build the PT however you like. You'll shine. Send me your progress by mail, I'll cover my parts.
beats.speaker: han

line: Yes, sir! Loyalty! I'm on my way.
beats.speaker: han

line: Isn't that the one they call the Peeper? Comes in early to watch the women arrive.
beats.speaker: gl

line: He begged to go to Ulsan. Said he had to know the machines he'd sell. Passionate? No. Showing off. They say he made a big mistake in front of a buyer there.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: A total dud. Who's going to be the bomb squad?
beats.speaker: gl

line: Jang is at the copier, humming.

A dream: a great player's hand, a veteran's face. Giants who talk while countless people listen, and him with his eyes and ears shut. Next to the board where you fight alone, the world seems kinder, and warmer.

On the train he scrolls his PT notes. The one thing he kept from giving up baduk is concentration. Right thinking shows the one proper move. The best of thought and experience: that's what baduk calls joseki. And he has sente. Build it however you like.
He mails Han three PT items and asks for feedback by tomorrow, then goes to lunch with the interns. Grilled mackerel. Pollack stew.
Picked yours? Not Jang, surely. Everyone thinks he's easy.
beats.speaker: gl

line: Easy? Who knows. Maybe a big dud. A nuclear bomb.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: In the afternoon lull, people read the news on the sly, or nap. Only the interns are still busy. He calls Han from the restroom.
You said I could build it my way.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: I said share it. I never said I'd keep my mouth shut. I know how this company works. Who should be listening to whom? I'm helping you.
beats.speaker: ms_han

line: In the next stall, the glasses intern heard every word. By evening it's everywhere: a dud hugging a dud.
The Ulsan plant. Han runs across the factory floor.
You begged, so you got one more chance. No mistakes. If you're not sure of yourself, go back to a desk and stop prancing round my site.
beats.speaker: ul

line: The department head mutters something as he goes. Han stands there, shaking.
Night, in Seoul. Stones spilled on the floor by an abandoned board, and Jang at his screen. The world is far colder, and more heartless.

Ulsan. In a fibre warehouse, the site's department head shows Han the bolts: strength, carbonisation, density. Leave that to the buyer's experts, he says. Your job is the samples and the papers, on the day, with no mistakes.
Han asks for help anyway. The old man softens. Buy me a soju when it's done.
Han rings Jang from outside the plant, cigarette in hand.
You call this a plan? An after-school hobby? Where I interned, I spent four days on one item. Twenty pages, packed tight.
beats.speaker: ms_han

line: Please check it. If it's short, I'll redo it.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Night, the lounge. He types alone. Forty-two pages. Forty. Fifty-three. More pages don't make it better; an item plan isn't a book report. He keeps going.
Morning. Oh, red-eyed, holds up a document Jang made for the team.

You should have followed the seniors' materials. Fixing it now won't help, I have to take this in and report! Colours that don't match, boxes all over the place, no order to any of it. What did you do yesterday?
beats.speaker: oh

line: The interns had the PT exam. They were short of time.
beats.speaker: kim

line: Sorry. Jang, can you fix it now?
beats.speaker: kim

line: Kim, under his breath: answer that fast and he gets angrier. He never got the time to be angry.
He yawns, eyes watering, and goes back to his desk.
He slips into an empty meeting room and calls Ulsan.
Interns are staff too, you know. Is this company work, or your own? Look at the size of it...
beats.speaker: ms_han

line: On the frame strip, Black's stones sit in the lower-left corner beside White's. Cho makes them solid first, then turns to fight.

Baduk is a fight at bottom, a war. You give way when pressed, sometimes you look to share the board, but the winner and the loser are plain. He lived in that world for over ten years. A beaten soldier, but raised to compete.
A player who doesn't hand over sente.
Then it's settled. We chose the item together, and you agreed to it. From here I write the PT, my way. I'll share the progress, but I don't take instructions. That's what we agreed, isn't it?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: A board covered in white stones. One of them falls to the floor.
After many short nights, he sleeps deeply at last: slumped in a chair in an empty meeting room.
All those items. Is he doing the PT alone?
beats.speaker: oh

line: His partner's Han Seok-yul, the one who went to the Ulsan plant. Han's a talker. I'd bet Jang's doing all the work.
beats.speaker: kd

line: A smooth talker, and one who can't tell he's being used. Some team.
beats.speaker: oh

line: He dreams of his heroes. Cho Nam-chul. Cho Hunhyun. Lee Chang-ho, Yoo Chang-hyuk. Lee Sedol. Cho Chikun, Segoe. One by one they fade. Don't go, he begs them. I'll do better.
My heroes are fading away. If they stayed, what could I do? Haven't I let go of baduk yet?
You were crying. And talking in your sleep. Picked your partner?
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Han Seok-yul. He's at the Ulsan plant.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: I've heard. Hungry for it. He'll use a weak partner to shine, and a strong one too.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: An ambitious man is a tornado. He wrecks everything round him. But the eye of a tornado is calm. Get into his centre, and you two could really work. Forget the gossip.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: I don't have that kind of skill.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: No. Your résumé's specialties box is empty. Shame insight doesn't count. You've got an unusual eye.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Still deciding. Nobody wants to team up with me.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Anyone good enough would work well with you.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Wait, that's why I came! The seniors have called all the interns out. It's evening. You slept the whole day.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Here to sleep, or to work? He's late. Three penalty glasses.
For the first time, he feels part of the team. The ones who use him, help him, get angry with him and scold him: all of them are on his side. Here, he is not an outsider.
With that, he ends today's baduk. Where the white stone fell from the board, there's a black one.
I've told you. Don't glue on top of other papers; it gets on the sheet underneath. Move it first.
beats.speaker: kd

line: And before anything goes in the scrap bin, check it isn't confidential. Figures, anything confidential: the shredder at the end of the floor. No paper of ours is ever found outside this team.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Kim Seok-ho, an intern on another team, hurries by.
Not yet. There are parts I don't get, and my section head's out on site.
beats.speaker: sh

line: The waybill copy and the payment details. Shred those?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: He'll wait for a few more approved papers and shred the lot at once. The yellow waybill stays on his desk: Sales Team 3, DH-14.
On my desk. Doesn't your team have any?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: The cabinet's locked, and nobody gives me the key. I have to beg every time.
beats.speaker: sh

line: At Jang's desk he glues his report pages flat, the waybill underneath. The glue soaks through. Late again, he scoops up his papers and runs, the waybill stuck to their back.
Jang gathers his pile and feeds the shredder, humming. He doesn't notice what isn't there.

Down in the lobby, Seok-ho finds the yellow sheet on his papers, tears it off and asks the security desk to throw it away. It slides off the counter onto the floor. A director stops beside it, and taps it with his shoe.
Director! Is this about a team dinner?
beats.speaker: oh

line: Without a word, the director kicks the team's paper box over. His aide hands Oh the waybill: found on the lobby floor.
Kim and Jang go down on their knees for the papers.
On the roof, a senior yells at a line of interns. Do they think they've got the job already? Focus!
At his desk, Oh turns the waybill over. Glued to it is a torn scrap of white paper. Weekly report. Internship. Kim Seok-ho.
Applause from across the floor. Go, a section head on Sales Team 1, comes over pumping his fists.

My baby intern, Kim Seok-ho! Drafts like a machine, all-nighters with us. Left another firm's internship because he wanted a real trading company. Newly married, and he barely goes home. Married young: eldest son of an eldest son. And we've just landed it.
beats.speaker: go

line: He comes to our team a lot. To borrow supplies.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Ha! My fault. The cabinet key's on my key ring.
beats.speaker: go

line: They grade interns on everything. Keep him from careless slips.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Results are what count. He did all our translating. ...The interns are off somewhere. Back soon.
beats.speaker: go

line: Oh looks at the folder in his hands. A locked cabinet. A borrowed glue stick. A waybill that walked.
By the copier, the interns troop back from the roof, groaning. Jang tells a staffer it was his fault: he left a waybill lying about, the director picked it up in the lobby, and everyone paid for it.
At the end of the day Kim is still on a shipping request. Oh takes the phone and bullies the buyer onto a container ship: the contract date doesn't move.
It isn't nine yet, and Oh is already tipsy.
No. Geu-rae did nothing wrong today.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Why dig it up? It's done.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Thank you. It was still my carelessness.
beats.speaker: jg

line: Go's team comes up the street, drunk on their win.
Jealous, Oh? You snub my intern over a few supplies, and now you want to spoil our win?
beats.speaker: go

line: Get your intern his own glue! Mine took the blame because yours got glue on a document and dropped it!
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Go doesn't take it in. Kim Seok-ho does.
He says he'll ring his wife, and goes back to drinking with his team.
Late, Kim Seok-ho comes home to one room. His wife has only just got to sleep. The baby is awake, and knows him. Dada. Her hand closes round his finger. He falls asleep beside them in his suit.
In another room, in the dark, Jang sets stones on a board, one at a time.

Incheon harbour, at first light. Cargo meant for Gunsan was unloaded here, some of it damaged, and he came to see it with his own eyes. The more you lean on paper, the further you drift from the site, until you have to take the other side's word for it.
He settles it with the forwarder and the insurer. Every arrival date has a few spare days in it; no real harm. A late breakfast. He's pleased with himself.
Back on the thirteenth floor, the air is tight. Kim Dong-sik waves him over to watch.

Steve Han: an American citizen, his family emigrated after middle school. Department head of the Americas textile team. Facing him, Kim Bu-ryeon, department head over Sales Teams 1, 2 and 3. The same rank. Steve has come onto Kim's floor to pick a fight, with everyone watching.
My team was up all night. You had the report on time.
beats.speaker: br

line: I don't have time for a report this thick. A fat report hands over every scrap so nobody has to take responsibility. A title means you take responsibility.
beats.speaker: st

line: We wanted to help you understand the situation.
beats.speaker: br

line: My job is selling textiles in the Americas. I need to understand the client, not your catalogue. Don't write me a thesis. Come and see me. Answer my questions.
beats.speaker: st

line: Stop making other people do your team's work. I don't care where the yarn came from. Who's it for? What climate do they live in? What taste went into the design? Just tell me what I need.
beats.speaker: st

line: Everyone is playing their own baduk, and wants to play the best moves they've prepared. Whoever prepared better is happier with the result. Whoever rushed to keep pace, and lost, has no excuse.
And Kim Bu-ryeon lost on his own ground, with a crowd to watch.
In a meeting room afterwards, Oh presses Go. Why would Steve lecture their department head on the basics?
Poor communication. He's picky. Too American.
beats.speaker: go

line: He spoke to us in Korean just now. Out with it.
beats.speaker: oh

line: The buyers came. Steve suggested dinner with my team, and I picked the place. I'd had a few. I told them this is how Koreans get friendly over work.
beats.speaker: go

line: How it happened. Over drinks at a dog-meat place, section heads from rival companies traded buyer stories. Plenty of foreigners love it, they said; more of them can't stand perilla leaves. Go envied their adventurous spirit.

So he took a buyer, and Steve, to a dog-meat restaurant. He read Steve wrong: a foreigner who wouldn't know, or a Korean at heart under the American passport. Steve saved the deal. Go never apologised, and his paperwork was sloppy, so Steve sat on Sales Team 1's approvals. Then Kim Bu-ryeon called him up to complain, and lost.
Go wanted to take Steve to a sauna and settle it man to man. I talked him out of it.
beats.speaker: oh

line: A sauna? Steve looks easy-going, but he's a very private man.
beats.speaker: kd

line: And our department head is too sore to apologise. In a way, it's checkmate.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Baduk words, from people who don't play. Jang grins.
You're laughing while your seniors talk?
beats.speaker: kd

line: If it's checkmate, you stop clinging to the stone. You give it up.
Apologising is the only way. In baduk they say don't leave dead stones on the board. Steve will do it again, and a dead stone left lying there grows into a bigger problem.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Easier said. He's proud, and he was shamed in front of his people. An office runs on politics.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Getting nervous over something this petty hurts his pride more. If it's politics, let's do it with class. Being humble when it counts: that's class. Let's go.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Kim Bu-ryeon isn't at his desk. He left scowling, someone says, with Go.
Behind a partition on the textile floor: Kim Bu-ryeon is already there, with Go. He got there first.
I didn't know what had happened. I'm sorry.
beats.speaker: br

line: And I'm sorry I lost my temper. Thank you for coming yourself. I expected Go to come alone.
beats.speaker: st

line: I was petty. I sulked. I'm sorry. ...So will the approvals go faster now?
beats.speaker: go

line: Often the obvious move is the hardest. Players lose games they could have won because they won't take the plain path, and each refusal tangles things further. Some things you must do however hard, and some you must not do however easy. He has seen it twice today: this morning, and now.
A dry sauna. Towels on wooden benches. Steve alone at the far end.
